paragraphs.text: The country now known as New Zealand is thought to have broken away from Australia about 65 million years ago, and it was not until the late 13th century that humans arrived there, having sailed all the way from other Polynesian islands. They lived in New Zealand as independent tribes and were only referred to as 'Māori' when European settlers arrived several hundred years later.

The earliest known dwellings constructed by the ancestors of modern-day Māori were Wharepuni adaptations of the houses they had known in their former homelands in Polynesia. The houses in their new country were originally designed and constructed to be temporary shelters, because the occupants were obliged to move frequently in search of food and other supplies. Often a group of 10 or more was built together around a large, clear space, with each one occupied by a single family group. This kind of grouping was referred to as a marae. For some as yet unknown reason, the elaborate stone marae structures of central and eastern Polynesia were not reconstructed in New Zealand. One explanation is that there was simply no time or resources to construct great stone monuments when faced with the extreme effort of establishing new communities in an environment unlike other Pacific Islands.

The earliest houses were built to a rectangular plan, but towards the end of the 14th century it was round houses that became the most favoured due to the simplicity of their construction. They had a wooden frame covered with reeds collected from river banks and palm leaves, and sometimes other materials such as tree bark. Houses also had to include several features designed to keep the occupants warm, as New Zealand's climate was significantly colder than the tropical Pacific. Researchers know that they were small and had a low door and few, if any, had window openings, to make them easier to heat. They were often either built partly below ground level, or were insulated by earth that had been piled up against the outside walls. An inside fireplace was used for heating and a simple opening near the roof allowed some smoke to escape, but any cooking was done in a separate building a small distance away that was shared by the whole settlement. Around the 15th century, as communities grew larger and more settled, more sophisticated buildings began to appear. These included the wharepuni (a sleeping house), in which several families could be accommodated each night. The wharepuni acquired a front porch – an outside sheltered area that separated the smoky, dark interior and the bright, outside world, so people entering could become accustomed to the change in light. This porch was not found in the houses of other South Pacific islands, and was a uniquely Māori adaptation to the climate.

Other buildings found in a Māori settlement in the period after the 15th century included the pātaka (storehouse). It had to be protected from predators such as rats so it was raised above ground level, often on one or more poles, with a removable ladder making it possible to climb up. Kept inside were prized objects such as different kinds of weapons, and nets and hooks that were used when the men went fishing. Pātaka often represented the wealth and status of a tribe, and in the 16th century, they began to appear more decorated. This was only possible due to a significant technological shift, which impacted on Māori architecture and art. From this time, wood cutting and carving tools were fabricated from greenstone which largely replaced other softer stone tools. Greenstone retains a hard and sharp cutting edge, and so carvers were able to carve far more intricate designs and patterns over doorways and windows.

The best-known structure built in accordance with Māori culture, however, is the whare whakairo (carved meeting house). This was typically a single large room with a pitched roof extended past the front wall to form an open porch. Most importantly, the meeting house was usually elaborately decorated, both inside and out, with representations of the ancestors of a particular tribe, who are much respected in Māori culture, and also with designs that were intended to be more abstract.

The front of the house was always built so that it faced the east, which is the location of Hawaiki (the Polynesian homeland) but also the direction of the sunrise, an event associated with renewal. It is not an ancient form of architecture, but first appeared after contact with Europeans in the mid-19th century at a time of social, political and spiritual change. These changes made it necessary for discussions to take place in a formal setting between communities – the native Māori and the recently arrived Europeans. Not all meeting houses are decorated, however. The use of imported materials and technologies, such as weatherboard, corrugated iron and nails, and the influence of European architectural forms, such as the church, led to the development of communal buildings that were western in appearance, but functionally Māori.

Nowadays, in the 21st century, building whare whakairo means combining traditional architectural practices with modern regulatory requirements for fire exits, adequate ventilation, plumbing and drainage. Sir Apirana Ngata, a key figure in Māori architecture, welcomed many of these innovations but believed, as do other architects in his field, that some building regulations 'have done enough mischief by compelling rows of windows where there were none, and letting light into places where it had no business to pry into’.
